articles.label: Public Records
articles.headline: Escambia County quietly settled five lawsuits last year. The terms remain sealed.
articles.dek: County attorneys invoked confidentiality clauses in settlements totaling an estimated $2.3 million. Commissioners say they weren't briefed on the details.
brief: Escambia County settled five civil lawsuits in 2025 with confidentiality agreements that shield payment amounts and case details from public disclosure.
At least three county commissioners told The Flightline they were not fully briefed on settlement terms before voting to authorize payments from the county's self-insurance fund.
Florida law permits confidential settlements involving government entities in limited circumstances, but transparency advocates say the practice undermines public accountability.
articles.body:
The meeting lasted eleven minutes.

On September 18, 2025, the Escambia County Board of County Commissioners convened in closed session to discuss pending litigation. When they emerged, they voted 4-1 to authorize a settlement in a case listed only as "Doe v. Escambia County" on the agenda. No dollar figure was read into the record. No explanation of the underlying claims. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh cast the lone dissenting vote.

"I wasn't comfortable with what I was being asked to approve," Bergosh told The Flightline in an interview last week. "The information provided was minimal."

That September settlement was one of five civil cases Escambia County resolved through confidential agreements in 2025, according to records obtained through a public records request filed in January. The county attorney's office confirmed the existence of the settlements but declined to provide payment amounts, citing confidentiality clauses negotiated as conditions of the agreements.

Based on partial documentation and budget records reviewed by The Flightline, the five settlements appear to total approximately $2.3 million drawn from the county's self-insurance fund. The county would not confirm or deny that figure.

What the records show

The Flightline requested all settlement agreements, releases, and related correspondence for civil litigation resolved in calendar year 2025. The county provided redacted copies of five settlement agreements. In each case, the payment amount, specific factual allegations, and names of individual county employees involved were blacked out.

County Attorney Alison Rogers said the redactions were required under the terms negotiated with plaintiffs' attorneys.

"These confidentiality provisions are standard in civil litigation," Rogers wrote in an email. "They protect all parties and allow for resolution without protracted and expensive trials."

The cases involved, according to the limited information provided:

  • An employment discrimination claim filed by a former Public Works employee
  • A wrongful termination suit brought by a former detention officer at the Escambia County Jail
  • Two personal injury claims related to vehicle accidents involving county equipment
  • A civil rights complaint stemming from an incident at a county facility, details unspecified

Rogers declined to elaborate on any of the cases beyond what appeared in the redacted documents.

Commissioners in the dark

Florida's Government in the Sunshine Law requires that settlement negotiations in pending litigation may occur in closed session, but the final settlement must be approved in a public meeting. What that approval process looks like in practice varies by jurisdiction.

In Escambia County, commissioners said they receive verbal briefings from the county attorney before closed-session votes. Written summaries are not standard. Three commissioners—Bergosh, Steven Barry, and Lumon May—told The Flightline they were not provided with itemized breakdowns of settlement costs or detailed explanations of the underlying facts before voting.

"We're told the broad strokes," said Commissioner May. "Whether the county has exposure, whether the attorney recommends settling. But I couldn't tell you today exactly what happened in most of those cases."

Commissioner Barry said he trusts the county attorney's judgment but acknowledged the process leaves gaps.

"I'm relying on counsel to tell me if we should settle," Barry said. "I don't have independent access to the case files. I'm not sure how I would even evaluate the underlying claims."

Commissioner Mike Kohler and Commission Chair Robert Bender did not respond to interview requests.

A matter of public money

The settlements were paid from Escambia County's self-insurance fund, a reserve account funded by taxpayer dollars and maintained to cover liability claims, workers' compensation, and legal judgments. The fund's balance at the end of fiscal year 2025 was approximately $14.6 million, according to the county's comprehensive annual financial report.

Withdrawals from the fund do not require line-item approval from commissioners. The county administrator has authority to process payments once a settlement is authorized.

Barbara Petersen, founder of the First Amendment Foundation and a longtime advocate for government transparency in Florida, said confidential settlements involving public funds raise serious accountability concerns.

"The public has a right to know how their money is being spent," Petersen said in a phone interview. "When a government agency settles a lawsuit, that's an admission that something may have gone wrong. Hiding the details doesn't make the problem go away—it just makes it invisible."

Florida law does permit confidential settlements in cases involving trade secrets, certain personnel matters, and situations where disclosure could compromise ongoing investigations. But Petersen said those exceptions are narrower than many government attorneys assume.

"There's a tendency to default to confidentiality because it's easier," she said. "But easier isn't the same as legal, and it's certainly not the same as right."

Patterns and precedent

Escambia County is not unique in its use of confidential settlement agreements. A 2023 survey by the Florida Center for Government Accountability found that 47 of Florida's 67 counties had entered into at least one confidential settlement in the preceding five years. The practice is particularly common in employment and civil rights cases, where plaintiffs often request confidentiality to avoid publicity.

But the same survey found wide variation in how counties handle disclosure. Some, like Orange and Hillsborough counties, adopted policies requiring public disclosure of settlement amounts regardless of confidentiality clauses governing other terms. Others, like Escambia, leave the decision to the county attorney's discretion.

The Flightline reviewed settlement practices in neighboring Santa Rosa County for comparison. Santa Rosa settled three civil cases in 2025. In each instance, the settlement amount was read into the public record during the commission meeting where the agreement was approved. Two of the three agreements included confidentiality provisions covering the underlying facts, but not the payment itself.

Santa Rosa County Attorney Roy Andrews said disclosing dollar amounts is standard practice.

"The public is entitled to know how much we're paying," Andrews said. "The details of the case can be confidential if that's what the parties negotiate. But the money? That's taxpayer money. It should be on the record."

What comes next

Commissioner Bergosh said he plans to raise the issue of settlement transparency at an upcoming commission workshop. He wants the board to consider a policy requiring public disclosure of all settlement amounts, regardless of confidentiality agreements on other terms.

"I'm not saying we should air every detail of every case," Bergosh said. "But the dollar figure should be public. Period. If we're paying out millions of dollars, the people who pay our salaries deserve to know."

County Attorney Rogers did not respond to a follow-up question about whether the county would support such a policy change.

The Flightline has filed a formal appeal under Florida's public records law challenging the redaction of settlement amounts. A response from the county is due by June 3.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Bluffs project promised 200 apartments by 2026. The lot is still dirt.
articles.dek: Three years after rezoning approval, the downtown development site at Main and Baylen sits empty. The developer blames rising construction costs. Neighbors blame the city for not enforcing deadlines.
brief: The Bluffs at Downtown Pensacola received rezoning approval in March 2023 with a projected completion date of late 2025.
Developer Coastal Vista Partners has not broken ground on the 200-unit apartment complex, citing a 34% increase in construction costs since approval.
Neighbors and city officials disagree on whether the project's conditional use permit should be revoked.
articles.body:
The chain-link fence went up three years ago. Weeds followed. Then came the hand-painted sign from a neighbor: "Future Home of Nothing."

The half-acre lot at the corner of West Main Street and South Baylen Street was supposed to hold a five-story apartment building by now. The Bluffs at Downtown Pensacola. Two hundred units. Ground-floor retail. A rooftop pool deck with views of Pensacola Bay.

On a Tuesday afternoon in May, the lot holds broken concrete, scattered beer cans, and a faded rendering of what might have been.

"We were told this would transform the block," said Rebecca Townsend, who lives in a duplex across Baylen Street. "My view transformed, all right. Into a trash pile."

The approval

Pensacola City Council approved the rezoning request for the Bluffs project in March 2023 on a 5-2 vote. The development required a shift from C-1 commercial to C-2A urban core mixed-use, which allows buildings up to 75 feet.

Council members who voted yes pointed to the city's stated goal of adding downtown housing density. Council member Delores Washington, who represents District 6, called it "exactly the kind of investment we've been asking for."

The conditional use permit came with stipulations. Construction was to begin within 18 months of approval. The developer, Coastal Vista Partners LLC, committed to reserving 15% of units as workforce housing, defined as affordable to households earning 80% of area median income.

Coastal Vista principal Marcus Embry told the council that night he expected to break ground by fall 2023 and deliver units by late 2025.

Neither happened.

The delays

Embry did not respond to three interview requests from The Flightline over two weeks. In a written statement provided through an attorney, he blamed market conditions.

"The construction cost environment has shifted dramatically since 2023," the statement read. "Lumber, concrete, and labor costs in Northwest Florida have increased approximately 34 percent. Financing terms have also changed materially. Coastal Vista remains committed to the Bluffs project and is actively working to secure revised financing that reflects current market realities."

The statement did not include a projected groundbreaking date.

Construction cost data from the Associated General Contractors of America shows a 28% increase in building material costs in the Pensacola metro area between March 2023 and March 2026. Interest rates on commercial construction loans have risen from an average of 6.2% to 8.7% over the same period, according to Federal Reserve data.

Other downtown projects have moved forward during that window. The Seville Quarter mixed-use development broke ground in 2024. A 48-unit apartment building on Palafox Place opened in January.

The enforcement question

The conditional use permit required construction to begin within 18 months. That deadline passed in September 2024.

City planning director Vanessa Morales confirmed that Coastal Vista requested and received a six-month extension in August 2024. That extension expired in March 2025. No further extensions have been granted.

"The permit is technically in violation," Morales said. "Revocation is one option available to the council, but it's not automatic. It would require council action."

Council member Washington said she has asked city staff to prepare a briefing on enforcement options but has not scheduled a vote.

"I'm not ready to give up on this project," Washington said. "But I'm also hearing from constituents who feel like they were sold something that isn't coming. We need to have an honest conversation about what's realistic."

Council member Jared Simmons, who voted against the original rezoning, said the situation validates his concerns.

"We gave away the store on height and density based on promises," Simmons said. "Now we have a hole in the ground and no leverage. This is exactly why I said we needed performance bonds, not just good intentions."

The neighbors

The lot at Main and Baylen sat vacant for years before Coastal Vista purchased it in 2022. It previously held a two-story office building demolished in 2018.

For a brief period after the 2023 approval, neighbors said they felt optimistic.

"I thought, okay, finally something's happening here," said Tom Guzman, who owns a small accounting firm on West Main. "Even the construction noise would have been better than watching it decay."

Guzman said he's now fielding complaints from clients about the state of the lot. Homeless encampments have appeared twice in the past year. The city cleared them both times after calls to code enforcement.

Townsend started a petition in February asking the council to revoke Coastal Vista's permits and rezone the lot back to C-1. The petition has 89 signatures.

"If they can't build it, fine," Townsend said. "Let someone else try. But don't let them just sit on it forever while the neighborhood suffers."

What's next

Morales said city staff will present options to the council at the June 12 meeting. Those options include revoking the conditional use permit, granting another extension with stricter conditions, or taking no action.

If the permit is revoked, the lot would revert to C-1 zoning, which limits buildings to 35 feet and does not allow residential use above the ground floor.

Coastal Vista would retain ownership of the property. The company paid $1.2 million for the lot in 2022, according to Escambia County property records.

Embry's statement concluded: "We understand the community's frustration. We share it. The Bluffs remains a viable project, and we are working diligently to bring it to fruition."

The fence around the lot has been there for 1,154 days. A city inspector visited on May 9 and cited Coastal Vista for overgrown vegetation. The company has 30 days to clear the weeds or face a $250 fine.

articles.label: NAS Pensacola
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 150,000 visitors. It also brings questions about who pays for crowd control.
articles.dek: Pensacola police and Escambia sheriff's deputies will work overtime through the weekend. The city expects reimbursement from the Navy. The Navy says that's not how it works.
brief: An estimated 150,000 spectators will attend this weekend's Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show at NAS Pensacola
Pensacola Police Department and Escambia County Sheriff's Office will deploy nearly 200 officers on overtime for traffic and crowd control
City officials expect Navy reimbursement for public safety costs, but Naval Air Station Pensacola says no such agreement exists
articles.body:
The line of cars on Navy Boulevard stretched past the Waffle House by 6:47 a.m. Friday. Parents in folding chairs. Kids with foam earplugs dangling from their necks. A man in a lawn chair had staked out his spot on the shoulder of Barrancas Avenue before sunrise, a cooler of Gatorade sweating beside him.

Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show weekend had begun.

By Sunday evening, Naval Air Station Pensacola expects 150,000 people to pass through its gates—the largest single event in Escambia County each year. The crowds will watch the Navy's flight demonstration squadron perform over Pensacola Bay, tour static aircraft displays, and buy $14 hamburgers from concession trailers.

What those visitors won't see is the small army of local law enforcement working the streets outside the base. Or the invoices that will follow.

The overtime question

Pensacola Police Department will deploy 47 officers on overtime assignments through the weekend, according to department spokesperson Kayla Morrison. Escambia County Sheriff's Office will have another 140 deputies working extended shifts for traffic control along Navy Boulevard, Blue Angel Parkway, and the surrounding residential streets.

The combined overtime bill will exceed $180,000, according to estimates provided by both agencies.

"This is our Super Bowl," said Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons at a press conference Wednesday. "We plan for it all year."

Who pays for that planning is less clear.

Pensacola City Administrator Keith Wilkins told city council members at their May 8 meeting that the city "historically receives reimbursement from the Navy for public safety support during the air show." He cited the arrangement as justification for approving the overtime expenditure without a formal budget amendment.

But when The Flightline contacted NAS Pensacola's public affairs office, spokesperson Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Foster said no such reimbursement agreement exists.

"The air show is a Navy event held on a military installation," Foster said. "Traffic control and public safety outside the gates is the responsibility of local jurisdictions, same as any other large event in the community."

A familiar dance

The disconnect isn't new. Similar questions arose in 2019, when city council member Sherri Myers asked for documentation of Navy reimbursements for air show security. City staff at the time could not produce a written agreement.

Myers, who left the council in 2020, said Thursday she never received a satisfactory answer.

"Every year it's the same thing," Myers said by phone. "The city assumes the Navy will cover it. The Navy assumes we're volunteering. Nobody writes anything down."

Current Pensacola City Council members did not respond to requests for comment Friday morning.

The Navy does provide some support. NAS Pensacola security forces handle all activity on base, and the installation coordinates with local emergency services for medical response. The base also opens additional parking areas and runs shuttle buses from remote lots.

But the miles of traffic cones, the deputies directing cars at intersections, the officers responding to fender-benders on Fairfield Drive—that's local.

The economic argument

Supporters of the current arrangement point to the air show's economic impact. A 2023 study commissioned by Visit Pensacola estimated the event generates $32 million in direct spending and supports 400 temporary jobs.

"You can't put a price tag on what the Blue Angels mean to this community," said Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves at the Wednesday press conference. "The return on investment speaks for itself."

But that return flows largely to hotels, restaurants, and retailers—not to the city's general fund. Pensacola's share of the tourism development tax goes to Visit Pensacola for marketing. The city's bed tax revenue won't be calculated until months after the weekend ends.

Meanwhile, the overtime bills come due in two weeks.

Escambia County faces the same math on a larger scale. The sheriff's office overtime costs alone will exceed $120,000, according to Chief Deputy Gregg Poteet. The county has no formal agreement with the Navy either.

"We've never asked," Poteet said. "It's just what we do."

What happens next

The air show will proceed as planned. The jets will fly. The crowds will cheer. The traffic will crawl.

By Monday morning, the cones will be gone and Navy Boulevard will return to its usual rhythm of fast food and pawn shops. The invoices will work their way through payroll systems. And the question of who pays will wait for another year.

Wilkins, the city administrator, said Friday he would "look into the reimbursement history" and provide documentation to council members at their June meeting.

"I'm confident we'll get this sorted out," he said.

Lt. Cmdr. Foster, at NAS Pensacola, was more direct.

"We appreciate the support of our local partners," she said. "We always have."

She did not say the Navy would be writing any checks.
